name: Su Tung-p’o
credit: Portrait of Su Shi (Su Dongpo) attributed to Zhao Mengfu (13th–14th century) · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Su Tung-p’o (Su Shi, 1036–1101) was one of the foremost poets of the Sung dynasty. Waley includes his well-known humorous quatrain written on the birth of a son.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poems.title: On the Birth of his Son
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)
poems.text:
Families, when a child is born
Want it to be intelligent.
I, through intelligence,
Having wrecked my whole life,
Only hope the baby will prove
Ignorant and stupid.
Then he will crown a tranquil life
By becoming a Cabinet Minister.

poems.title: Spring Nights
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898)
poems.text:
One half-hour of a night in spring is worth a thousand taels,
When the clear sweet scent of flowers is felt and the moon her lustre pales;
When mellowed sounds of song and flute are borne along the breeze,
And through the stilly scene the swing sounds swishing from the trees.

poems.title: Whigs and Tories
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898)
poems.text:
Thickly o'er the jasper terrace flower shadows play;
In vain I call my garden boy to sweep them all away.
They vanish when the sun sets in the west, but very soon
They spring to giddy life again beneath the rising moon!

poems.title: Dreaming at Golden Hill
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Feast of Lanterns (1916)
poems.text:
The stranger merchants faring from the east
Muffled in cotton robes, have met to feast.
They drink, they revel, and they part at will,
While moonlight floods the towers of Golden Hill.
The third watch comes, the tide begins to flow;
A fair wind follows, and in dreams I blow
The reed-pipes, and have sailed to far Yangchow.

poems.title: At the Kuang-Li Pavilion
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Feast of Lanterns (1916)
poems.text:
Red-skirted ladies, robed for fairyland, all have flown,
But my heart to the wail of their long reed-pipes lilts on:
Their clarion songs ’mid the wandering clouds were blown,
The tiny-waisted, dreamily-dancing girls are gone.

poems.title: Farewell to Chao Tâ-Lin
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Feast of Lanterns (1916)
poems.text:
Long do I sorrow that the spring should end;
Fain is the host to stay the parting friend.
When for a while the dull routine is done,
We statesmen idle in the sun.
The kettle yields its stream of golden tea,
And warm winds spread the odours of congee.
Finished the cup, faded the crimson peach,
Twilight, the green embankment levelled to the beach,
My boat is poled along the shore and soon
In the pure night unlanterned we recline;
Until, caps off to conquering wine,
We nod, the dream companions of the moon.

poems.title: On the River at Hui-Ch’ung
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Feast of Lanterns (1916)
poems.text:
Beyond the twilight grove some sprays
Of peach-bloom charm the lingering days.
In spring, when first the waters warm,
The wild duck on the river swarm.
When artemisia lights the land
Young reeds break through the dappled sand.

poems.title: Listening to the Playing on a Lute in a Boat
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: Chinese Poems (1912)
poems.text:
In my boat I sat alone,
  And the hours were fast in flight,
When the sound of music broke
  The stillness of the night.

Sighing winds through fir-trees swept,
  Falling cascades murmured low,
As the master touched his lute--
  So lovingly and slow.

Clutching fast my lapelled coat,
  Rapture swayed me without bounds,
As with every nerve intent,
  I listened to the sounds.

Yet again I longed to hear
  Ancient chimes on jadestone bell,
Drawn forth by the Master's hand
  From lute he loved so well.

Since the days of Chen and Wei,
  When confusion filled the land,
Music rare of ancient style
  Has found but scant demand.

Times and instruments alike,
  For a thousand years and more,
Silent and forgotten lay,
  And few the loss deplore!

One alone--the priceless lute--
  Change and storm and wreck survives,
Watching nations rise and wane,
  As god of mortal lives.

Music old is now decried,
  Light songs and ditties sought,
Strains insipid, jerky turns,
  Light and crispy wrought.

Instruments of wood remain,
  Void of human feelings sweet,
Which the soul of ancient song
  Never more may greet.

Peaceful is the river now,
  Moon-beams play upon the scene,
From the ceaseless din of life
  Night provides a pleasant screen.

In the silence of this hour,
  Will you, Master, yet once more,
Wen-wang's melodies revive,
  As in the days of yore?

poems.title: Night on the Lake
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: Chinese Poems (1912)
poems.text:
The breeze is sighing through the water grass,
As up and down the narrow deck I pass;
And through the rarest mist of Autumn night
The rain-moon floods the lake with pallid light.

The boatmen and the water-fowl sleep sound,
And in their dreams see other worlds around;
The big fish startled sneak in haste away,
As flurried fox flees from the dawning day.

In depths of night it seems the human soul
Its sway o'er other things has lost control;
I and my shadow play upon the strand
That marks the boundary of the silent land.

We watch the secret tides in noiseless work,
Forming new isles where earthworms safely lurk;
And on the moon--a monstrous pearl--we gaze,
Looming through willow-trees in silver haze.

Amidst our life of changing grief and woe,
A glimpse of purer worlds will come and go,
As on this lake when nature's holy power
Speaks to us in the dark and silent hour.

But hark, the cock crows; rings the temple bell!
And birds awake in mountain, plain, and dell;
The guardship beats its drum, the boats unmoor,
While din and shouting on the hearer pour.

poems.title: 水调歌头 (Shui diao ge tou)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
明月几时有，把酒问青天。
不知天上宫阙，今夕是何年。
我欲乘风归去，又恐琼楼玉宇，高处不胜寒。
起舞弄清影，何似在人间。
转朱阁，低绮户，照无眠。
不应有恨，何事长向别时圆。
人有悲欢离合，月有阴晴圆缺，此事古难全。
但愿人长久，千里共婵娟。

poems.title: 水龙吟 (Shui long yin)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
似花还似非花，也无人惜从教坠。
抛家傍路，思量却是，无情有思。
萦损柔肠，困酣娇眼，欲开还闭。
梦随风万里，寻郎去处，又还被、莺呼起。
不恨此花飞尽，恨西园、落红难缀。
晓来雨过，遗踪何在，一池萍碎。
春色三分，二分尘土，一分流水。
细看来，不是杨花点点，是离人泪。

poems.title: 永遇乐 (Yong yu le)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
明月如霜，好风如水，清景无限。
曲港跳鱼，圆荷泻露，寂寞无人见。
如三鼓，铿然一叶，黯黯梦云惊断。
夜茫茫，重寻无处，觉来小园行遍。
天涯倦客，山中归路，望断故园心眼。
燕子楼空，佳人何在，空锁楼中燕。
古今如梦，何曾梦觉，但有旧欢新怨。
异时对，黄楼夜景，为余浩叹。

poems.title: 洞仙歌 (Dong xian ge)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
冰肌玉骨，自清凉无汗。
水殿风来暗香满。
绣帘开、一点明月窥人，人未寝、枕钗横鬓乱。
起来携素手，庭户无声，时见疏星渡河汉。
试问夜如何，夜已三更，金波淡、玉绳低转。
但屈指、西风几时来，又不道、流年暗中偷换。

poems.title: 卜算子 (Bo suan zi)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
缺月挂疏桐，漏断人初静。
时见幽人独往来，缥缈孤鸿影。
惊起却回头，有恨无人省。
拣尽寒枝不肯栖，枫落吴江冷。

poems.title: 青玉案 (Qing yu an)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
三年枕上吴中路。
遣黄耳、随君去。
若到松江呼小渡。
莫惊鸥鹭，四桥尽是，老子经行处。
辋川图上看春暮。
常记高人右丞句。
作个归期天已许。
春衫犹是，小蛮针线，曾湿西湖雨。

poems.title: 临江仙 (Lin jiang xian)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
夜饮东坡醒复醉，归来仿佛三更。
家童鼻息已雷鸣。
敲门都不应，倚杖听江声。
长恨此身非我有，何时忘却营营。
夜阑风静縠纹平。
小舟从此逝，江海寄馀生。

poems.title: 定风波 (Ding feng bo)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
莫听穿林打叶声。
何妨吟啸且徐行。
竹杖芒鞋轻胜马。
谁怕。
一蓑烟雨任平生。
料峭春风吹酒醒。
微冷。
山头斜照却相迎。
回首向来萧瑟处。
归去。
也无风雨也无晴。

poems.title: 江神子・江城子 (Jiang shen zi / Jiang cheng zi)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
十年生死两茫茫。
不思量。
自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡。
小轩窗。
正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年断肠处，明月夜，短松冈。

poems.title: 贺新郎 (He xin lang)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 宋詞三百首 (Three Hundred Song Lyrics)
poems.text:
乳燕飞华屋。
悄无人、桐阴转午，晚凉新浴。
手弄生绡白团扇，扇手一时似玉。
渐困倚、孤眠清熟。
帘外谁来推绣户，枉教人、梦断瑶台曲。
又却是，风敲竹。
石榴半吐红巾蹙。
待浮花、浪蕊都尽，伴君幽独。
艳一枝细看取，芳心千重似束。
又恐被、秋风惊绿。
若待得君来向此，花前对酒不忍触。
共粉泪，两蔌蔌。

poems.title: 春宵 (Chun xiao)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
春宵一刻值千金，花有清香月有陰。
歌管樓臺聲細細，鞦韆院落夜沈沈。

poems.title: 上元侍宴 (Shang yuan shi yan)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
淡月疏星繞建章，仙風吹下御爐香。
侍臣鵠立通明殿，一朵紅雲捧玉皇。

poems.title: 海棠 (Hai tang)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
東風嫋嫋泛崇光，香霧空濛月轉廊。
只恐夜深花睡去，故燒高燭照紅妝。

poems.title: 花影 (Hua ying)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
重重疊疊上瑤臺，幾度呼童掃不開。
剛被太陽收拾去，卻教明月送將來。

poems.title: 西湖 (Xi hu)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
畢竟西湖六月中，風光不與四時同。
接天蓮葉無窮碧，映日荷花別樣紅。

poems.title: 飲湖上初晴後雨 (Yin hu shang chu qing hou yu)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
水光瀲灩晴方好，山色空濛雨亦奇。
欲把西湖比西子，淡妝濃抹總相宜。

poems.title: 冬景 (Dong jing)
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: 千家詩 (Poems of a Thousand Poets)
poems.text:
荷盡已無擎雨蓋，菊殘猶有傲霜枝。
一年好景君須記，最是橙黃橘綠時。
